items.title: 68357_Jimmy Maxwell oral history interview
items.q: And Ashby said, I think he was serious, says, "I don't know anything about that solo." And Dave and I looked at him, sort of in amazement.

ctx.x: Well, it came about I had written -- transcribed some arrangements for Mercer Ellington that had been lost after Duke's death. And one was on "Congo Brava" and Ben Webster made a classic tenor solo that was famous with most musicians. And I had just written in the chord symbols, I didn't write it out. And a friend of mine, Dave Burger (PHONETIC), had copied the arrangements, and Harold Ashby, who's a great tenor sax player and a great friend of Ben Webster's, was going to play the solo.

And then Dave said to him, well, Jimmy didn't transcribe Ben's solo, but I guess you know it if you want to play it. And Ashby said, I think he was serious, says, "I don't know anything about that solo." And Dave and I looked at him, sort of in amazement. I said, 'how come you don't know it?' And then in other incidents, the fact that you don't find young -- you know, you don't see young black musicians playing like Louis, or anything.

I thought about it a great deal and the explanation seemed to me, and I think it's likely, the young black musician is not interested historically that -- he doesn't have the time, he doesn't have the money. Most musicians, black or white, I think, come from poorer circumstances. But the historical aspect of music and jazz is a hobby that takes money to follow. And the young black musician coming up is interested in playing like contemporary musicians that are successful, because he's got a very pressing problem,…
